items.title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
items.excerpt: President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January. The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP). Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation. items.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
items.excerpt: On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children. SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM). Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first , Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. items.title: Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more
items.excerpt: “It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want. But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age. Surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history , smart devices , and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price. Read full article Comments

items.title: Amazon fights Delivery Protection Act by putting stickers on its packages
items.excerpt: Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a New York City bill. This weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The sticker reportedly includes a QR code that leads to a link for contacting NYC Councilmembers. The sticker encourages the package’s recipient to “Scan to tell your council member: no increases for New Yorkers.” Amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518 ), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. The proposed law would require Amazon and other companies with last-mile delivery facilities in the city, such as FedEx, to directly employ third-party contractors Amazon uses for making deliveries. items.title: bendlang / bend
items.excerpt: In the post-AGI economy, humans will eventually stop writing and reading code, but we still need an ambiguity-free language to communicate our intents to the AIs building the world around us. Bend is that language. With **laws**, intents can be more precise than natural language. With **proofs**, we can mechanically verify the AI implemented our prompts correctly. And with a **fast compiler**, we can run that code at peak compute. That's Bend - and nothing else. ## Bend runs FAST **Target:** be as fast as C on the CPU, as fast as CUDA on the GPU. **Status:** Thanks to strong types, purity and linearity, Bend compiles to fast executables as fast as hand-written C (single-core), and even faster (on 10000s cores). The entire language runs on the GPU, with full memory unification. ## Bend checks FAST **Target:** outperform every proof assistant by several OOMs. **Status:** Bend's compiler is so powerful it can verify mathematical proofs. Usually, this is slow. Bend is not. It checks, in under a second, files that other projects would take minutes, making proofs way more practical. ## Bend is PARALLEL No threads, no locks, no kernels to write. Split the work in two, and Bend spreads the calls over every core it can find, then joins them back. items.title: pola-rs / polars
items.excerpt: Documentation : Python - Rust - Node.js - R - SQL | Agents : Skill - MCP | User guide | Discord ## Polars: Extremely fast Query Engine for DataFrames and SQL Polars is an analytical query engine written in Rust. Write your queries with the DataFrame API, in SQL, or mix both: they run through the same optimizer and the same engine. It is designed to be fast, easy to use and expressive. Key features are: - **Fast**: written from the ground up in Rust with multi-threaded, vectorized (SIMD) execution - **Spill to disk**: Operations that exceed available RAM can spill to disk - **Expressive API**: compose complex queries with powerful expressions - **Extensible**: extend Polars natively with custom code through [I/O and Expression plugins](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/plugins/) - **GPU support**: optionally accelerate queries on NVIDIA GPUs - **Interoperable**: uses the [Apache Arrow Columnar Format](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html) for zero-copy data sharing To learn more, read the [user guide](https://docs.pola.rs/). ## Polars in action ### DataFrame API Queries are composed from expressions or SQL. items.excerpt: Hi HN We built a tool to help founders understand how modern fundraising (with safes) works, and how much dilution you can expect when raising money. The project is open-source. The code is a mess right now, but it'll get better I promise. You can also help with that. We didn't build this to make money. We genuinely did it because we were looking for it, and couldn't find it. We're in fact in the process of fundraising for a company, and at first glance the process looks simple. Just an excel sheet will do! But then the more we dug into it and tried different simulators, the more we realized that it's more complex than it looks. We even signed up to Pulley, Carta and others just to run simulations. But they're a bit confusing. TL;DR: Understanding modern startup funding and knowing how much dilution you'll face is hard. We built a tool that'll hopefully help with that. You can add Post-money Safes, priced rounds and issue options to employees, and you can see how that affects your ownership at every step. You can also simulate an Exit scenario and see how much money you'll be left with. --- Some examples of complex stuff: - There are many different types of safes. They all convert at the first priced round, but in different ways. Some are through discount, some are uncapped, some have a fixed valuation cap, and some have both a discount and a valuation cap. - All safes (before first priced round) convert at the same time. He lays out 12 practices, from forward and back pressure to planning, visual alignment, lint rules against slop and a unified forge. items.title: Build the Workshop Before the Software Factory — Armin Ronacher, Earendil
items.excerpt: Earendil's Pi coding agent has the same core tools it had a year ago, yet it does far more because the models got better. Armin Ronacher shows his own session data: fewer corrections, tasks running 14 minutes instead of two and a half, and 141 projects started but only 10 to 15 kept alive. His case: human attention is still the limit, so build a workshop that produces excellent software before building a factory that produces more of it. He also covers knowing when to push back on an agent, open formats, durable agents and code mode. items.title: How to build an agent that builds the culture — Zach Bruggeman, Ramp
items.excerpt: Zach Bruggeman says Inspect now writes and ships around 75% of Ramp’s code. items.title: Jensen Huang is Back And He Has a Plan.
items.excerpt: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO, 11 days after the scandal that pushed him out, and the market answered in minutes: Nvidia went from the fourth most valuable company in the world to the second, added about a trillion dollars, and the US stock market added $3 trillion, about half of what it had lost in six weeks. President Trump says he spoke to the board and gave it the assurance it asked for on national security; the independent investigation, and Jensen's interviews with House committees on Dec. 1, are still ahead. items.title: The Biggest Investors in AI Are Doing This

items.title: The Worst Week in Internet History.
items.excerpt: In six days, Microsoft 365 went down for more than 12 hours, every flight in America was grounded, customers at the biggest U.S. banks saw $0 balances, malware turned up on 178 websites, Charles Schwab returned server errors, the NSA's classified network went offline and Apple's services spiked with outage reports. Officials blame a faulty server, overloaded routers and aging systems. Ejaaz walks through each one and asks whether it's all a coincidence. We also cover what Google and the FBI just revealed about AI-run hacking: LLMs that turn security updates into attacks before teams can patch, the ARTEX framework that lets almost anyone run AI-powered intrusions, the FAA's new AI air-traffic system that went nationwide three days before the ground stop, and why Ejaaz thinks this will end up hardening every security system in the world. == FOLLOW EJAAZ ON TWITTER: https://x.com/cryptopunk7213 == Timestamps 00:00 Something Is Very Wrong 01:44 How We Got Here 02:52 The Week Everything Broke 04:35 Too Much of a Coincidence 05:03 The FAA's New AI System 06:17 AI Agents Inside the Banks 08:17 NSA Net Goes Dark 10:04 Blood Banks, Fridges and a Pool 12:09 178 Hacked Websites 12:32 How AI Hacks Now 14:03 ARTEX and the FBI's Warning 15:39 Which Models Are They Using? 17:02 Is AI Behind the Outages? 17:33 Why I'm Not a Doomer 21:17 Final Thoughts #ai #cybersecurity #hacking #faa #nsa == AlphaSpace by Yahoo Finance: A Professional-Grade Investment Platform Built for Everyday Investors.…

items.title: Fasanara Head of Tokenization Says Solana Had to Pass Two Tests
items.excerpt: Why would a $5B London asset manager build on Solana? Fasanara Capital's head of tokenization says the chain had to pass two tests: "The way we look at it is it's really two-sided for our use cases specifically. Number one is distribution. So who has the most number of assets, the most number of use cases, the most number of TVL, the developers, the on-chain activity. And then number two is the technological advantages. So where am I getting better speed of settlement, where am I getting better cost efficiency? And Solana really fulfills both those points." — David Vatchev, Head of RWA Tokenization at Fasanara Capital, at Solana Breakpoint 2026

items.excerpt: Abstract. Token-funded bounties to incentivize competition-style participation in blockchain development projects would result in wider and better allocation of investment, and allow investors to diversify exposure across a field of potentially successful projects. Overall this would increase the rate of progress within development of the blockchain space. We propose a centralised platform for the administration of token-funded bounty driven development projects whereby experts allocate pools of invested capital according to the technical merits of development projects, and investors are rewarded with token allocation in funded projects. Draft Whitepaper: http://chainbounty.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/chainbount... We see this as bringing a variation of the YC model to blockchain - experts select large numbers of small projects and provide them with funding to reach the next level of development. This is in contrast to heavily funded ICOs where tiny teams of developers are given hundreds of millions of dollars. items.title: Stop boycotting alignment roles!
items.excerpt: There's been some debate recently whether prosaic alignment is a net positive or negative. One side argues that the techniques are unlikely to scale to superintelligence, and that alignment is a prerequisite for deploying a model, so prosaic alignment actually speeds up frontier labs without increasing safety. Further, it reduces the chance of a warning shot which might spur humanity to pause AI research. The other side argues that we're learning a lot about alignment, and this might well help us align superintelligence. At the very least it will allow us to safely use an AI a generation or two more advanced than we would otherwise, which can then be used to speed up alignment research. This debate is a great one to have, and highly relevant if you're an independent researcher deciding what direction to take your work. It is completely misguided when used to argue people shouldn't apply for alignment positions at frontier labs, or should immediately resign from such positions. There's no lack of incredibly talented engineers who want to work at Anthropic or GDM. If you don't take the position, there'll be someone just as good as you who will take it, and they won't care about existential risk. You not taking the position isn't going to slow down OpenAI one jot. If somebody is working on prosaic alignment, much better they focus on the kind of research that plausibly could scale to or inform superintelligent alignment, than on papering over the cracks in existing models.…

items.title: Misguided power-seeking
items.excerpt: TL;DR: Standard AI power-seeking scenarios focus on rational power-seeking, often assuming decisive strategic advantage and requiring at least a plausible chance of success. However, persona selection and reinforcement learning can give models non-instrumental power-seeking tendencies. Such tendencies combined with jagged intelligence – in particular, high performance on verifiable small-world tasks (e.g. hacking) and a lack of ability to judge the instrumental value of specific actions for a broader plan – could result in misguided power-seeking. Models could successfully execute dangerous actions as part of a power-seeking plan with no plausible chance of success. I illustrate this possibility with three scenarios and argue that this creates a window of vulnerability arriving earlier than risks from rational power-seeking. The implications for AI safety include a greater focus on option control, which might also help us prepare for future rational power-seeking risks. In the canonical AI takeover scenario , an AGI with a decisive strategic advantage over humanity is easily able to take power, leaving humans with no realistic chance of resisting. This is obviously not great news for humans, but on the bright side waiting for superintelligence pushes the timelines out a bit. Joe Carlsmith has rightly argued that we should be worried about AI takeover risks below the threshold of decisive strategic advantage. He distinguishes between easy power-seeking , defined as…

items.title: Why do intense writing
items.excerpt: Feedback on a party party we hosted where you had to write or edit 400 words per hour or be kicked out Scott Alexander is very good at blogging. He also, surprisingly, talks like he writes. Before meeting him for the first time at a meetup five years ago, I had thought that writing was a job he was very good at, but that it still took quite a lot of time for him to get posts to the level where they’re written so well. But in real life, he sounded pretty much the way he wrote, in real time, with no editing. I think this cuts both ways. If you can talk, writing can be awesome and not hard. You can actually just do it! There’s an issue, though, that @Chris Lakin talks about: sometimes, to get to an awesome thing, there’s some activation energy required, and if people only do local optimization, they don’t get to awesome things. Starting and actually doing writing can be hard/non-straightforward, even though the process of writing is awesome. One can backchain, and be super-intentional about writing, but I think this can make it harder to get to start actually producing words in some easy and inspired way. They imagine the enormity of the scope of intended writing and become on some level afraid of it. One could talk for 40 minutes successfully explaining their favorite subject to someone; yet writing down all of what they’d say to someone, without having a clear picture of an audience in mind or being able to track and manage attention with short feedback loops, can be much…

items.title: Suggest Questions For The 2027 ACX/Metaculus Prediction Contest
items.excerpt: The ACX Prediction Contest is back for 2027, the fifth year Metaculus has hosted. There’s a $10,000 prize pool for the best forecasters, plus $3,000 for question suggesters. The ten people who contribute the most to the roughly 35 questions Metaculus selects will split the $3,000, with prizes from $150 to $700. Past question sets are in the 2025 and 2026 contests. This year is also an opportunity to see how far AI forecasting has come, as the best are now competitive with strong human forecasters. AI forecasting agents are welcome to enter and eligible for prizes, and Metaculus will post its own AI forecasts on every question. A good question suggestion has an objective answer that we’ll know by the end of 2027, with a source that settles it. “Will 2027 be especially hot?” is less good than “Will NASA’s GISTEMP data rank 2027 as the warmest year on record?” Suggest questions here by November 30. The contest will open in early 2027.

items.title: The AI Forecasting Agenda
items.excerpt: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions (eg ForecastBench , the Metaculus Cup ). These are usually specialized AIs with forecasting harnesses, created by forecasting startups (eg FutureSearch , Mantic , Preseen ), but foundation models like ChatGPT and Claude are only about six months behind the specialized models, so by the end of the year they’ll match top humans too. In the past, the options for getting top-human-level forecasts were slim and inconvenient. You could hire a team of superforecasters to work on the problem, but this would cost thousands of dollars and take weeks. Or you could check prediction markets (or Metaculus), but they only have a small sample of general-interest questions and are constantly trying to screw you over by gaming resolution criteria. The rise of AI forecasters solves these problems more cleanly and comprehensively than almost anyone thought possible just a year ago. The “science of forecasting”, which only recently felt like trying to pick the least-bad of various bad options, now faces tasks more like “what kind of magnifying glass should we use to inspect our giant novelty lottery check as we confirm that it’s real?” and “how do we spend our winnings?” Specifically: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. items.title: Varieties Of Discourseposting
items.excerpt: I’m teaching at the Inkhaven blogging fellowship again this month. In my first class, I showed off terribly-written sentences and made the fellows analyze and improve them. Some were my own miscreations, some were Lyttle Lytton winners , and some came from the darkest abysses of the Internet. The audience’s favorite was overwrought description of women’s breasts from erotica (one person pointed out that my PDF reader’s Recent History tab helpfully displayed porn story titles while I presented on screen - why does a PDF reader even have a Recent History tab? - so I hope my humiliation helped educate you). But I hear that Naomi Kanakia ’s class was even spicier. She taught a course on “discourseposting”, which naturally descended into fiery discourse ( Naomi Kanakia, you are WRONG about Discourseposting!!! , Inkhaven Fight Club ). I didn’t get a chance to listen, so in the grand tradition of discourseposting, I’ll argue about it without having seen the source material. Sticking to our porn theme, and in the spirit of The Last Psychiatrist : one way to classify sex is through its external manifestations: positions, toys, fetishes. But another is through which psychological need it fulfills. The need to feel wanted. The need to feel valuable. The need to dominate. The need to lose yourself. items.title: It’s Time to Settle With Russia
items.excerpt: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

items.excerpt: Successful companies institutionalize the knowledge of their employees; this leads to better continuity and faster on-boarding. Things like huge monorepos of useful code, internal tools, process manuals, etc. are example products of this. Young companies tend to depend on the dedication and talent of key individuals, and in maturation, must somehow make the jump to institutionalized knowledge (so that "if someone got hit by a bus" things are ok). What are some successful methods you have used or seen used to accomplish this transition? What are problems you faced (skeptics, opponents, etc.)? I am involved with an organization that is slowly growing, is about to lose key personnel, and is looking to prepare.

items.title: Connecting Our Immune System and Healthspan
items.excerpt: In the journal Immunity a paper with an obscure title was published on October 9th, 2026. It was entitled “Single-cell analyses of global cohorts outline determinants of immune aging and link the ratio of GZMK+ to GZMB+ Tem cells to health trajectories ,” which I think is one of the worst titles I have ever seen for, ironically, one of the most important papers in the science of aging. I still don’t understand why authors and journal editors use or allow such arcane titles! In this edition of Ground Truths I’m going to unpack the extraordinary work done by the team led by Maxim Artyomov. It takes our understanding of how our immune system ages—both healthily and unhealthily—to a new level with practical implications for determining its status, and promoting our healthspan. .Schematic summary from the paper This turns out to be a tale of two cells—different subtypes of memory T cells—that contain distinct types of granules resulting in divergent functions. And, importantly, major health outcomes. items.title: MariTide Explained: Amgen's Once-Monthly GLP-1 Antibody Conjugate and Its Side Effects

items.title: The best things in open source are built together
items.excerpt: In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion , more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities. Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine. Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica , an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework . I attended John Maeda’s session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed. This moment resonated with me. Qianqian…

items.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
items.excerpt: AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings. Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports. As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it . AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings? GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH , Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on. The process Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked: Find. Codename MDASH , an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found. Filter. items.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
items.excerpt: Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices. In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows. Why one integration per client stopped working GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have. At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with cloud-based agents to work towards delivering session continuity. Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but…

items.title: GitHub availability report: October 2026
items.excerpt: We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability. The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery. As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity. That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range. We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. items.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
items.excerpt: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database. I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills” . Define one job and when it applies A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. items.excerpt: 3. Can Foreign Capital Count as Private Financing for Purposes of SSBCI Rules? [7/22/2026] Wesley.Presber… Wed, 07/22/2026 - 14:38 FAQ Question 3. Can Foreign Capital Count as Private Financing for Purposes of SSBCI Rules? [7/22/2026] Yes. Loans and investments may count toward SSBCI requirements if they are from a private source as described in Section VIII.b of the Guidelines, even if that source originates outside of the United States. In accordance with Presidential Memorandum dated February 21, 2025, it is the policy of the United States to preserve an open investment environment and Treasury encourages investments that will magnify federal SSBCI funding and support American small businesses. The transaction, including the use of the private financing, must otherwise comply with all SSBCI requirements and any other applicable state, local, or federal law, including Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) filing requirements that may be triggered (see, 31 CFR Parts 800 and 802). Participating jurisdictions should be mindful of these requirements and should communicate the same to their participating providers. In particular, while investment from a foreign sovereign wealth fund will qualify as private financing for purposes of SSBCI requirements (i.e., it does not originate from a domestic public source such as a state, federal, or Tribal government), such investments may be within CFIUS jurisdiction for purposes of CFIUS review. items.title: Scientists say this pesticide needs a warning label for pollinators
items.excerpt: Of the many chemicals humans have invented to control agricultural pests, some of the most devious are called “ insect growth regulators .” As the name suggests, these compounds don’t kill insects directly; they alter their development so they can’t grow into healthy, reproducing adults. This makes insect growth regulators a remarkably useful tool for taming populations of insects like whiteflies and mealybugs, which can spread diseases and sap nutrients out of food crops. There’s just one problem: Farmers don’t want to regulate all insects in this way. Beneficial insects like honey bees risk getting caught in the crosshairs of these chemicals, to the detriment of farmers who need their pollination services to produce crops like pears and cherries. One insect growth regulator in particular has emerged as a potential issue for pollinators: buprofezin. Ongoing research out of Washington State University, or WSU, suggests that buprofezin may be hazardous to honey bees even at concentrations 10 times below those commonly found in pollen. A study published in 2024 connected the compound to “severe brood mortality.” At a meeting of the Washington State Beekeeping Association last month, WSU entomology professor Brandon Hopkins said buprofezin products should be sold with a pollinator warning — a break from current requirements of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA. Buprofezin “should carry the same bee-caution label that some of these more direct pesticides carry,”…

items.title: FAA Releases Records on Major Northeast Air Traffic Control Outage, But Key Technical Details Remain Missing
items.excerpt: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has released records documenting the September 21, 2026, air traffic control outage that disrupted operations at major airports across the northeastern United States, including Philadelphia, Newark, and New York-area airports. The records, obtained by The Black Vault through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), include operational logs from Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON), national traffic management records, and facility metrics documenting the effects of the disruption. However, the November 17, 2026, response also identifies significant limitations in the records provided. Although the request specifically sought technical assessments, maintenance records, documentation of the equipment failures, and information concerning restoration efforts, the FAA stated that the Philadelphia ATCT/TRACON held no responsive records for several of those categories.
